title: When Federal Funding Cuts Reach Refugees’ Everyday Lives
displayTitle: When Federal Funding Cuts Reach Refugees’ Everyday Lives
subtitle: How the 2025 suspension of refugee admissions and federal funding changes contributed to CWS Orange County’s closure—and what that means for refugees’ everyday lives in Southern California.
excerpt: After CWS announced its Orange County office would close, I traced how the suspension of refugee admissions and federal funding changes contributed to the decision, and what the closure means for families relying on help with housing, benefit applications and everyday life in Southern California.

content.caption: Residential buildings in Long Beach, California. Illustrative photograph.

content.text: In July 2026, Justin Castillo, the senior case manager and volunteer coordinator at CWS Orange County, asked me to assist a refugee family in finding an apartment in Long Beach, closer to work. He would provide the leads to the family.
On July 17, I provided him with a preliminary spreadsheet with the information on potential housing. Application requirements were to be verified, and Justin coordinated the search with the family.

Almost a month later, on August 14, Justin announced that Church World Service would close its Orange County office on September 4. Most of the staff, including him, would finish their employment on that date, and the volunteer work would officially come to an end.

The closure email cited changes in federal policy and funding, including the suspension of the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program and the changes in federal grants and funding that went through other organizations. As fiscal year 2027 (FY27) approached, he described the situation in Orange County as a “devastating fiscal cliff.” I was interested in how the decisions on admitting refugees impacted the office working with refugees already in the United States.

content.alt: The U.S. Capitol beneath a blue sky.
content.caption: The U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C. File photograph.

content.text: The policy changes cited in the closure email began more than a year earlier. On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14163, "Realigning the United States Refugee Admissions Program," suspending refugee entry through the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program effective January 27 and suspending decisions on refugee applications. The order allowed case-by-case exceptions. It justified the policy by citing public safety, national security, community capacity, and preservation of taxpayer resources.

On that day, President Trump signed another order, the Executive Order 14169, directing the review and pause of foreign development assistance. In response, the State Department issued stop-work notices on January 24 for resettlement agreements, including services delivered domestically. On February 26, it notified the resettlement organizations of the termination of their cooperative agreements effective February 27. While the admissions order restricted the entry of refugees, the subsequent actions of the agencies impacted the funding of organizations providing assistance to people already admitted.

In their June 2026 amended complaint, CWS and the other plaintiffs described the reimbursement per refugee as partly covering direct aid and partly covering service costs and overheads. When the reimbursement is tied to arrivals, fewer arrivals result in less income supporting the agency's operation. A payment freeze creates a separate issue, as an organization can incur expenses that it expects to be reimbursed by the government.

In May 2025, CWS announced its plans to close 11 local offices, citing the changes in federal policy and the loss of support. Orange County was not among them. CWS later reported that some of the services resumed on May 23 and that most of the outstanding federal funding and reimbursements were released.

In Pacito v. Trump, CWS joined other organizations and individuals contesting the administration's actions. On March 5, 2026, the Ninth Circuit largely reversed the preliminary relief concerning the refugee admissions and processing, while preserving the relief against the suspension of domestic resettlement funding. The opinion also distinguished the agencies' domestic funding decisions from what the executive orders directed.

The government cited the restored funding in an August 11, 2026, filing, arguing that the domestic funding claim should be dismissed because the suspension was not expected to recur. This litigation position does not establish the financial condition of each office operating within the resettlement network.

According to the amended complaint, an Iraqi refugee living in Dallas, identified in the case by the pseudonym Ali, arrived in January 2025 with $120. The local agency helped him arrange an apartment. On February 5, he received the notification that Refugee Cash Assistance payments would face an indefinite delay, which his case manager attributed to the federal funding suspension. The complaint cites his fear of losing housing. It also mentions that he later received the resettlement benefits after the court's injunction.

Orange County participated in the programs beyond initial refugee reception. According to the listing of California's Department of Social Services, CWS Orange County provides services under the Ukrainian Newcomers Support Program using the federal Ukraine supplemental appropriations provided through state grants. The listed services include case management and housing navigation. The state gives the program an end date of September 30, 2026.

The program's end date was close to the office's closure date. Neither the state listing nor the closure email specifies the amount of this grant in the office's budget. The published end date does not prove that the administration canceled the grant prematurely. CWS attributed the closure to several policy and funding changes; the available records cannot reconstruct the office's budget.

My understanding of the wind-down process was that all the previously promised assistance, including the housing search, security deposits, and assistance with the benefit applications, would be completed as the service arrangements came to an end. I could not confirm that all the payments and handoffs had been completed.

CWS could assist someone with navigating a CalFresh application, while Orange County's Social Services Agency administered the benefit. The closure of a CWS office did not terminate a person's eligibility.

CWS's public closure notice states that the work begun in Orange County will continue through its Northern California office. It does not specify which clients will receive which services, who will handle their cases, or whether the arrangements will be remote or local.
For the Long Beach family, I can document the housing search and Justin's coordination. I cannot yet confirm whether they found an apartment or who assisted with their remaining needs.
Justin's closure email gave volunteers and clients an opportunity to stay in touch if both parties wished to do so, as community members rather than CWS volunteers.

reportingNote: I volunteered in housing navigation with CWS Orange County. This article follows the policy and funding changes cited in its closure announcement, drawing on my correspondence with staff and public records from government agencies, the courts and CWS.
